kapak.alt: Impedance matching and middle ear gain

youtube.baslik: Why Do We Need a Middle Ear? Impedance Matching | Lesson 29 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
When sound passes from air into the fluids of the inner ear, most of its energy is reflected. In this lesson, we look at how the middle ear makes up for this loss: the areal ratio, the ossicular lever, the total gain and its clinical importance, with a sample audiogram.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Gelfand, Hearing: An Introduction to Psychological and Physiological Acoustics; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology; Pickles, An Introduction to the Physiology of Hearing; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.baslik: Why Do We Need a Middle Ear? *Impedance* Matching
sahneler.alt: Impedance matching, the areal ratio and the ossicular lever
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson, we learn why the middle ear is needed, through the idea of impedance matching.
Step by step, we will calculate the areal ratio, the ossicular lever and the total gain of these mechanisms.

sahneler.baslik: When sound passes from *air* to fluid
cumleler: Sound reaches our ears from the outside world through air molecules.
The cochlea, however, is filled with fluids called perilymph and endolymph.
So before it becomes a neural signal, sound has to pass from air into fluid.
Fluid is much denser than air and resists being set into vibration far more strongly.
That is why most of the sound energy that tries to pass directly from air into fluid is reflected back at the boundary.
This is one reason why, under water, we can hardly hear someone talking at the edge of the pool.
Impedance is the total opposition a system offers to the energy we try to transfer into it.
The denser and stiffer a medium is, the more force is needed to set it vibrating.
Acoustic impedance has three components: mass, stiffness and friction.
The impedance of air is low, while that of the inner ear fluids is very high.
Reducing this mismatch so that energy passes efficiently between two media is called impedance matching.
This is exactly the main job of the middle ear.

maddeler.metin: Energy passed: only _one in a thousand_

yan.metin: Without a middle ear, about *30 dB*

cumleler: The acoustic impedance of fluids is thousands of times that of air.
With such a large mismatch, about ninety nine point nine percent of the sound energy is reflected at the boundary.
Only about one thousandth of the energy passes into the fluid.
An energy ratio of one in a thousand corresponds to a loss of about thirty decibels.
So without a middle ear, sounds would reach the inner ear about thirty decibels weaker.
The middle ear works like a transformer that makes up for most of this loss.
The middle ear is an air-filled space between the tympanic membrane, or eardrum, and the inner ear.
The malleus is attached to the tympanic membrane, and the incus follows the malleus.
The last link of the chain is the stapes, the smallest bone in the body.
Together, these three bones are called the ossicles.
The footplate of the stapes sits in the oval window, which opens into the inner ear.
In this way, vibration collected by a large membrane is delivered to a much smaller window.
This arrangement is the basis of the most powerful mechanism of impedance matching.
The first and most important mechanism is the areal ratio, also called the hydraulic effect.
The effective vibrating area of the tympanic membrane is about fifty five square millimeters.
The total area of the membrane is larger, but not all of it vibrates with the same efficiency.
The area of the stapes footplate is about three point two square millimeters.
The ratio of the two areas is about seventeen to one.
When force collected over a large surface is concentrated onto a small one, the pressure per unit area increases.
Think of a thumbtack: pressing on its broad head lets the sharp tip go in easily.
The areal ratio alone provides a gain of about twenty five decibels.

etiketler.metin: long process of incus: short arm

cumleler: The second mechanism is the ossicular lever.
The manubrium, the handle of the malleus, is slightly longer than the long process of the incus.
When the ossicles rotate together like a lever, this difference in length increases the force reaching the stapes.
With the lever, the movement of the stapes becomes slightly smaller, but its pushing force becomes larger.
The lever ratio is about one point three to one.
This ratio means an extra gain of about two decibels.
The gain may look small, but it multiplies with the areal ratio and adds to the total effect.
Now let us put the two mechanisms together: the areal ratio provides about twenty five decibels.
The ossicular lever adds about two decibels to this.
Seventeen times one point three is about twenty two, which is a gain of around twenty seven decibels.
Sources usually give the total gain as twenty five to thirty decibels, depending on the calculation and measurement method.
This value is quite close to the roughly thirty decibels lost at the air to fluid boundary.
So the middle ear makes up for most of the loss, though not all of it.

maddeler.metin: Curved membrane: a small extra gain

cumleler: Some sources note that the curved shape of the tympanic membrane also creates a small extra lever effect.
The middle ear also directs sound mainly to the oval window.
Because the round window is shielded behind the tympanic membrane, the two windows do not receive the same pressure at the same time.
This phase difference is needed for the cochlear fluids to move effectively.
Finally, the Eustachian tube keeps middle ear pressure equal to the outside air, so the membrane can vibrate freely.

ogeler.metin: _Mass_ dominates: the weight of the system

cumleler: The middle ear does not transmit every frequency with the same efficiency.
At low frequencies, the stiffness of the system, its resistance to stretching, governs transmission.
At high frequencies, mass, the weight of the system, becomes more important.
In healthy adults, the resonant frequency of the middle ear is usually between eight hundred and twelve hundred hertz.
So problems that increase stiffness tend to affect the low frequencies, and those that add mass tend to affect the high frequencies.
We will use this relationship in detail later, in the immittance lessons.
When there is a perforation, or hole, in the tympanic membrane, the effective area that collects sound becomes smaller.
The hole can also reduce the shielding of the round window; the loss depends on the size and location of the hole.
In otosclerosis, the stapes footplate becomes fixed to the oval window by new bone, and vibration transmission is reduced.
When the ossicular chain is disrupted, the lever system is put completely out of action.
The aim of middle ear surgery is often to rebuild this transformer system.
The common result of these conditions is a conductive hearing loss, seen on the audiogram as an air-bone gap.
In this sample audiogram, the air conduction thresholds of the right ear are around sixty dB HL.
The bone conduction thresholds measured with masking are in the normal range, so the right cochlea appears to work well.
The difference of about fifty five decibels between them is a large air-bone gap.
In this example, the left ear is within normal limits.
When the ossicular chain is disrupted behind an intact tympanic membrane, the conductive loss can reach about sixty decibels.
This is because an intact membrane, without the lever effect, also largely stops sound from reaching the windows directly.
This example is close to the upper limit of conductive loss; a full evaluation is made together with the ENT physician.

sahneler.metin: If the air-bone gap clearly exceeds about 60 dB, first check bone conduction masking, vibrator placement and calibration.
cumleler: A tip from practice: conductive hearing loss has a physiological upper limit.
If the air-bone gap clearly exceeds about sixty decibels, the result is larger than expected.
In that case, first check bone conduction masking, the placement of the vibrator and the calibration of the equipment.
This is because undermasking can measure bone conduction from the opposite ear and make the gap look larger than it is.

maddeler.metin: Energy is _reflected_ from air to fluid

cumleler: When sound passes from air into the inner ear fluids, most of its energy is reflected; this is a loss of about thirty decibels.
The step from a large membrane to a small window, the areal ratio, provides the largest gain.
The ossicular lever adds a small but meaningful contribution to this gain.
With a gain of about twenty five to thirty decibels, the middle ear largely makes up for the impedance mismatch.

sahneler.soru: What contributes most to middle ear gain?
sahneler.aciklama: The areal ratio of about _17:1_ between eardrum and footplate gives about 25 dB on its own.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: Which mechanism makes the largest contribution to the gain provided by the middle ear?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: the areal ratio.
The ratio of about seventeen to one between the eardrum and the stapes footplate gives a gain of about twenty five decibels on its own.
